You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Shadow

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, 'shadow' most commonly symbolizes divine protection and refuge — being sheltered under God's presence, pictured as resting in the shadow of His wings or of the Almighty. God's shadow represents nearness, covering, and safety for those who trust Him.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Psalm 91:1 (abiding under the shadow of the Almighty)",
    "Psalm 17:8 (hide me under the shadow of your wings)",
    "Psalm 36:7 (children of men take refuge in the shadow of your wings)",
    "Psalm 57:1 (in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge)",
    "Psalm 63:7 (in the shadow of your wings I sing for joy)",
    "Psalm 121:5 (the LORD is your shade at your right hand)",
    "Isaiah 25:4 (a shade from the heat, a refuge from the storm)",
    "Isaiah 49:2 (in the shadow of his hand he hid me)",
    "Song of Solomon 2:3 (I sat down under his shadow with great delight)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Typological foreshadowing: Old Testament laws, rituals, and institutions as a 'shadow' of the reality (substance) found in Christ and heavenly things — the shadow-versus-substance contrast central to Christian typology.",
      "basis": [
        "Colossians 2:16-17 (these are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ)",
        "Hebrews 8:5 (a copy and shadow of the heavenly things)",
        "Hebrews 10:1 (the law has but a shadow of the good things to come)"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Transience and brevity of human life: shadow as an image of fleeting, insubstantial existence.",
      "basis": [
        "Job 8:9 (our days on earth are a shadow)",
        "Job 14:2 (he flees like a shadow and does not continue)",
        "1 Chronicles 29:15 (our days on the earth are like a shadow)",
        "Psalm 102:11 (my days are like an evening shadow)",
        "Psalm 144:4 (his days are like a passing shadow)",
        "Ecclesiastes 6:12 (life passed like a shadow)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Death, darkness, and gloom: 'the shadow of death' (tsalmavet) as an image of mortal danger, deep darkness, or spiritual gloom from which God delivers.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 23:4 (the valley of the shadow of death)",
        "Isaiah 9:2 / Matthew 4:16 (those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has dawned)",
        "Luke 1:79 (to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death)",
        "Job 10:21-22 (the land of darkness and the shadow of death)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Changeability and instability contrasted with God's immutability: God has 'no variation or shadow due to change,' making shadow a symbol of mutability and inconstancy.",
      "basis": [
        "James 1:17 (with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Conveyed divine power or presence through a person: shadow as a medium of healing or overshadowing power.",
      "basis": [
        "Acts 5:15 (Peter's shadow falling on the sick)",
        "Luke 1:35 (the power of the Most High will overshadow you)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "False or unreliable security: the shade of human alliances or rulers as inadequate protection compared with God's.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 30:2-3 (seeking shelter in the shadow of Egypt shall be your humiliation)",
        "Judges 9:15 (take refuge in the shade of the bramble)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "Shadow is a genuinely polyvalent biblical image with no single settled symbolic meaning; interpretation is context-dependent. Two meanings compete for primacy: (1) devotional/Old Testament usage strongly favors protection and refuge under God, and (2) doctrinal/New Testament usage strongly favors the typological shadow-versus-substance contrast (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 8:5; 10:1), which is arguably the most distinctively Christian theological use of the term. Reference works such as the Dictionary of Biblical Imagery typically list protection, transience, and foreshadowing as parallel senses rather than ranking one as definitive. I have listed protection as primary because it is the most frequent scriptural usage, but the typological sense is at least equally prominent in Christian theological teaching, so it is marked dominant among the alternatives."
}

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The symbolic meaning of a shadow is highly context-dependent in Scripture. In the Old Testament, it primarily contrasts the heat of the sun (danger, judgment) with shade (divine protection), or illustrates how quickly human life passes. In the New Testament, it serves a critical theological function distinguishing the anticipatory shadows of the law from the substantial reality of Christ."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "A preliminary, incomplete foreshadowing or type of the greater spiritual reality fulfilled in Christ. Christian interpretation especially describes the Mosaic law, sacrifices, festivals, priesthood, and earthly sanctuary as “shadows,” while Christ and the new-covenant realities are the substance.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Colossians 2:16–17 — food laws, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths are “a shadow of the things to come,” while the substance belongs to Christ.",
    "Hebrews 8:4–5 — the earthly priests and sanctuary serve “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.”",
    "Hebrews 10:1 — the law has “a shadow of the good things to come” rather than their full reality.",
    "Hebrews 9:23–24 — the earthly sanctuary is treated as a copy of the heavenly reality, supporting the same shadow-and-fulfillment framework."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Divine protection, refuge, and nearness, especially being sheltered under the shadow of God’s wings.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 17:8",
        "Psalm 36:7",
        "Psalm 57:1",
        "Psalm 63:7",
        "Psalm 91:1",
        "Isaiah 32:2"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Mortality, transience, or the fleeting and insubstantial character of human life.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Chronicles 29:15",
        "Job 8:9",
        "Job 14:2",
        "Psalm 102:11",
        "Psalm 109:23",
        "Psalm 144:4",
        "Ecclesiastes 6:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Deep darkness, mortal danger, suffering, or death, traditionally expressed as “the shadow of death.”",
      "basis": [
        "Job 3:5",
        "Job 10:21–22",
        "Psalm 23:4",
        "Psalm 44:19",
        "Psalm 107:10",
        "Isaiah 9:2; compare Matthew 4:16 and Luke 1:79"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Change, instability, or variation, used negatively of God, with whom there is no shifting shadow.",
      "basis": [
        "James 1:17"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A vehicle or sign of extraordinary apostolic healing power, based on people hoping Peter’s shadow would fall on the sick.",
      "basis": [
        "Acts 5:15–16"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a settled dominant theological use of “shadow” in Christian typology: an anticipatory and inferior form that points to fulfillment in Christ. The word is nevertheless context-dependent across Scripture and does not carry that meaning in every occurrence; protection, transience, and death or danger are also well-established biblical metaphors."
}

RESPONSE D
{
  "primary_meaning": "A temporary, incomplete, or typological foreshadowing of a greater spiritual reality (especially Christ, the gospel, or heavenly things)",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Colossians 2:16-17",

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Biblical usage of 'shadow' is strongly context-dependent; the typological sense is especially prominent in Christian theological interpretation of Old Testament institutions, while protective and death-related senses dominate in the Psalms and prophetic literature. No single meaning monopolizes Christian teaching."
}

BOOK ENTRY
An object or activity shaped like the substance casting it, marking the reach and boundary of that substance's covering. The appointed times and holy assemblies are the Shadow of Christ's substance; the Shadow of Death is its opposite.
[.opposite]Opposite: Shadow of Death.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ps 91:1; Num 14:9; Col 2:16-17; Heb 8:5; 10:1; Lev 23:2-4) · see Shadow, ch. 17

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Psalms 91:1 — He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Numbers 14:9 — Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
Colossians 2:16 — Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
Colossians 2:17 — Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Hebrews 8:5 — Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
Hebrews 10:1 — For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
Leviticus 23:2 — Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, Concerning the feasts of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations, even these are my feasts.
Leviticus 23:3 — Six days shall work be done: but the seventh day is the sabbath of rest, an holy convocation; ye shall do no work therein: it is the sabbath of the LORD in all your dwellings.
Leviticus 23:4 — These are the feasts of the LORD, even holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
